conclusion: The suggested claim is false for every prime: omitting an odd prime p from S caps the number of occupied residue classes mod p, not |A| (counterexample: any A inside 1 + pZ), and only p = 2 caps |A|, at 2. The descent the arm asked for exists (g*(k) <= 2^k for primitive A, by deleting one odd prime, tight at k = 1, 2) but its per-prime loss provably cannot go below 2: the residue relaxation that parity, residue classes, prime deletion and the power-of-2 lemma all factor through has optimum exactly 2^k.
confidence: Lean hard on the refutation and on the descent lemma: both are short proofs with explicit witnesses re-verified by trial division. Lean hard on the obstruction too, but only for what it says, which is that no bound below 2^k follows from (R1)+(R2); it says nothing about g(k) itself. The one place not to lean is the general case: Theorem 4 covers primitive sets only, and the divisible part A_p = {a : p | a} escapes the descent because (S, pA) is admissible whenever (S, A) is. Nothing here improves the classical 3*2^(k-1).
